en: Folios 1–4 are missing. I.
I would cause [someone] to adopt an evil view.

Then, at that very moment, Māra the Evil One quickly vanished from his own abode and, assuming the appearance, dress, and deportment of the venerable Aśvajit, stood in the middle of the road before those two noble men and spoke as follows.
Indeed, I have previously stated that this reason given by way of analogy is false; for what purpose do you two wish to know the regulation of the movement of your own minds?
All of this that has been said is indeed useless, for there is no further reason for it here.
Whence could there be the attainment or the fruit of this auspicious deed of Kṛṣṇa here?
O you two, who indulge excessively in the qualities of desire, enjoy your play quickly!
"There is no death, nor birth; there is no world beyond, nor suffering and old age;
nor does there exist the fruit of merit or demerit produced by karma, nor the causal efficacy of action here.
The son of the Śākyas speaks thus for the sake of gain; do not follow him out of faith. RKP 1.10
Then this thought occurred to Upatiṣya and Kaulita:
"Alas, this is surely Māra the Evil One who has approached us for the purpose of dissuading us from our renunciation."
Then Upatiṣya, turning his back [on the assembly], called his own circle together and spoke thus:
"Listen, young men; remember the defects of saṃsāra!
The world is oppressed by old age and surrounded by death."
"For the sake of abandoning both of these, you should properly undertake the life of renunciation.
Then Kaulita spoke to Māra:

The noble Dharma, known by the wise and possessing intelligence, which brings an end to the three types of suffering— there is nothing whatsoever that could ever distract us from this resolve. With steadfast minds, we are always intent upon the complete pacification of craving.
"Do not, with the form of a lion and the words of a jackal, cause us to wander from our resolve.
And those deities who had seen the truths, stationed in the sky, gave their approval to those two noble beings:
"Excellent, excellent, noble beings! This path is indeed distinguished above all the world, namely, the departure into the life of renunciation."
This path is the pacification of all suffering;
this path is the entry into the domain of all Tathāgatas;
this path—namely, the going forth and renunciation—is praised and extolled by all the Blessed Buddhas.
Then indeed, Māra the Evil One, distressed, dejected, and full of regret, vanished right then and there.
Then the two wandering mendicants, Upatiṣya and Kaulita, looked at their own assembly and spoke thus:
"O young men, you should know that we have set out for the renunciant life under the Tathāgata in order to reach the further shore of the ocean of old age and death.
However, whoever among you does not wish to go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, let him turn back right here."
And all those five hundred young brahmins said this:
"Whatever we know, all that is through the power of you two.
Surely you two have gone forth into the religious life in a noble state."
"Whomever you two have set out to follow by going forth, we too shall go forth for his sake."

Then, knowing that the two wandering mendicants Upatiṣya and Kaulita, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, had set out for the sake of going forth under the Blessed One, Māra the Evil One manifested a great abyss outside the great city of Ājagṛha,
extending a hundred yojanas in depth.

Thinking, "In such a way that those two will not be able to approach Śravaṇa Gautama," the Blessed One again performed such a feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) that the two wandering mendicants, Upatiṣya and Kaulita, did not see that great precipice as they traveled along the straight path.

Again, Māra the Evil One manifested a mountain before the two of them, [a mountain] many hundreds of yojanas in extent, with a hollow a thousand yojanas deep and a thousand yojanas in height; he also manifested a thousand fierce, wicked, and terrible lions. Yet, through the majesty, power, and spiritual influence of the Blessed One, those two noble beings did not see even that mountain, nor the lions, nor did they hear the roar of the lions.
And by the straight path, they approached the place where the Blessed One was;
and the Blessed One, surrounded and honored by an assembly of many hundreds of thousands, was teaching the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, do you see these two virtuous men, the leaders of a group and surrounded by a retinue? They said: "We see them, Blessed One."
We see it, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"These two virtuous men, together with their retinues, having gone forth in my presence, one shall become the foremost among all my disciples endowed with wisdom, and the second shall be the foremost among those possessing supernatural powers."
Then, at that time, a certain monk spoke these verses:

"These two wise men, who were prophesied by the Benefactor, the Supreme among Men, and who are endowed with supernatural power and wisdom and are confident, have come here; I approach them, filled with reverence. Then that monk, rising from his seat, together with many monks and many householders and renunciants, went out to meet those two holy men and attended upon them.
Then those two virtuous men approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and standing before the Blessed One, they said this to him:
"May we both receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of monks in the presence of the Blessed One."
"Let us two practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."
The Blessed One asked,
"What are your names, noble sons?
Upatiṣya replied:
I am the son of the brahmin Tiṣya, named Upatiṣya;
my mother’s name is Śārikā,
and from her I was born.
Therefore, Śāriputra, the name "Śāriputra" was given to me;
I had previously been permitted by my parents to go forth into the religious life.
Kolita said,
"My father's name is Kauṇḍinya;
therefore, my name is Kaulita."
"My mother's name was Mudgalā;
therefore, the common name Maudgalyāyana was given to me. Some people know me as Kaulita."
"Someone named Maudgalyāyana," [he replied].
I have previously been granted permission by my parents to go forth into the religious life.
The Blessed One said, "Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, together with their retinues, are practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) in my presence.
That itself was their going forth (pravrajyā), their full ordination (upasaṃpad), and their status as monks (bhikṣubhāva).
And Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, together with their retinues, had recently gone forth [into the religious life].
Then Māra, the Evil One, assuming the form of Maheśvara, stood before the Blessed One and spoke as follows.
Those who are skilled in the study of the meanings of the treatises and have reached the further shore of the sciences—all of them bow at my excellent feet; I am their leader.
O Gautama, come today quickly to my refuge along with your assembly of disciples.
"I shall explain to you that path which leads to abundant and complete nirvāṇa.
The Blessed One said:
(Kurumiya 7)
Your path carries this world toward miserable rebirths and leads it into the ocean of suffering;
yet my path dries up the ocean of suffering for this entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
Why do you prattle so much more, you who are as audacious and talkative as a jackal?

"You are shattered; you are no longer able to perform the work of Māra against me here. Then Māra the Evil One, having made his form as Maheśvara disappear, stood again before the Blessed One in the guise of Brahmā and spoke thus.
O Sage, you who by means of your wisdom have crushed the sprout of existence born of karma and afflictions— why do you still exert yourself here for the sake of sentient beings?
O Lord, there is no person anywhere in this world who is a more worthy recipient than you.
"Why, being free from illness, do you not enter nirvāṇa quickly? For this is the time.
The Blessed One said:
"I behold beings who are incomparable, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Those who stand as my disciples, out of compassion they shall be fully liberated by me;
having reached the states of middling, superior, and inferior, the world shall be brought to final liberation.
"I shall enter nirvāṇa; why then do you invite me with such guile, O evil-minded one?

(RKP 1.17) Then again, Māra the Evil One, distressed, dejected, and full of regret, vanished from that very spot and went to his own abode. Entering a chamber of sorrow, he sat down. At that very moment, all the beings dwelling in the realm of Māra asked one another:
What is the reason that our great king has entered the chamber of sorrow and sat there, yet no one knows of it?
Then five hundred daughters of Māra, bringing most delightful flowers, garlands, and ointments,
and having adorned themselves with most charming garments and ornaments, played divine musical instruments that produced supreme and heart-gladdening joy;
dancing, singing, and playing with most enchanting voices, they performed with a great divine orchestra of fivefold instruments.
While engaged in amorous play, they stood before Māra, the Evil One;
and that Māra, the Evil One, stretching out his arms, began to cry out:
"Make no sound! Make no sound!"

When they had been addressed thus, those apsarases remained silent for a moment; then, singing once more, they struck their musical instruments. And Māra, the Evil One, again raised both his arms and began to cry out, until seven times those apsarases [performed] that dance fixed upon pleasure... again.
Māra the Evil One likewise raised both his arms and cried out:
"Make no sound! Make no sound!"
Having been addressed thus, those apsarases remained silent.
Then, the apsaras named Vidyudvalgusvarā, having joined her palms in reverence toward Māra the Evil One, spoke thus:
"O Lord, what sign of your own passing has been seen by you here today?
Or has the world today become as if engulfed by a consuming fire?"
"Is there some enemy here whose strength exceeds yours, that you, filled with sorrow, take refuge [with someone else]? Māra said:
I have a powerful enemy, the son of the Śākyas, whose mind is subdued and whose intellect is trained in illusions on this earth;
if there is no way at all to destroy him, then it is thus.
"He will empty my realm of desire here.
That celestial nymph said:
"Lord, by what means, powers, vigor, and prowess?"
Who here today would be able to bring about its ultimate and complete destruction—
that [suffering] which has long been the bond for the three realms of existence?
He is capable of exhausting the ocean of craving through his power.
Māra said:
"The noose of his intention for the vow of giving, his compassion, and his resolve—"
Holding a bow grasped by the supreme emptiness and signlessness,
he is the teacher who instructs the complete cessation of existence,
and he is favorable toward the tranquility of the path leading out from saṃsāra.
His disciples dwell in empty villages and cities, in the depths of forests, and even in mountain caves;
their minds are intent on meditation, and they lead lives of seclusion.
Constantly and according to rule, they were applied for the sake of exhausting the defilements;
accompanied by supernatural power, strengths, and compassion, Upatiṣya and Kaulita were disciplined by the Sage.
"By means of all the methods of the three worlds, he who is well-disciplined in the Dharma will indeed empty my realm of desire. Then,

having heard the praise of the Blessed One’s virtues from the presence of Māra the Evil One, those five hundred daughters of Māra all attained the bodhisattva-samādhi named "Lightning Devoid of All Forms."
Having obtained [this],
those five hundred daughters of Māra then cast divine musical instruments,
as well as divine flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, ornaments, decorations, and finery toward where the Blessed One was, for the purpose of worshipping the Blessed One.
And by the supernatural power of the Blessed One, those divine musical instruments and all those ornaments rained down upon the Bamboo Grove.
Then those daughters of Māra, together with their retinues, saw this for themselves;
having seen it, they were once again filled with serene joy, thinking, "Such a rain of flowers has fallen right here in the Bamboo Grove!"

Then those monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Blessed One: "Blessed One, regarding these two, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, together with their retinues— for whom such a great, wonderful, and marvelous rain has fallen, the likes of which was never seen or heard before—
what indeed, Blessed One, is the cause here?"
"What is the cause?
The Blessed One said,
"This is not due to the power of these two sons of good family."

But from that abode of Māra, the Evil One, five hundred female attendants released this kind of great rain of flowers, up to a rain of ornaments, for the sake of making an offering to me; before long, they will come here and receive the prophecy of their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment from my presence.

(Kurumiya 12) Then those five hundred Māra-maidens, having themselves heard the utterance of the sound of the Blessed One’s speech, developed even greater faith toward the Blessed One; and by that joy of faith, they—
They attained the samādhi called "non-forgetfulness of the thought of awakening."

Then those daughters of Māra, having adjusted their robes over one shoulder in that abode of Māra, placed their right knees upon the ground, joined their palms in reverence, and looking toward the direction in which the Blessed One was dwelling, spoke as follows:
O sole eye of the entire world, who dries up the river of craving and beholds the whole universe as a world deprived of sight—
you are today the savior of the world, including its humans and gods.
O Sage, how may we quickly become Buddhas here?
O Blessed One, worshiped by men and gods, speaker of the ultimate truth, having cast off this loathsome female state, may we all [become so].
O Lord of supreme intelligence, by means of your miraculous power, go quickly to his presence so that we may hear the words of the Lord of Sages;
O Blessed One, speaker of selflessness, seer of the ultimate truth!
O bearer of the jewels of the factors of enlightenment, lamp of stainless speech,
peerless one, having overcome the host of Māra, [protect] us!
"Now, grant us all together the prophecy for swift awakening!
Then, indeed, the daughters of Māra rose from their seats and, with one voice, spoke thus to Māra, the Evil One:
O you of wicked mind, how is it that you, having become corrupt in the presence of the Blessed One, have obtained this fleeting and unsubstantial body,
which is entirely afflicted by the sufferings of birth and the rest?
You have fallen into a terrible state, being arrogant with pride;
therefore, cast away your anger and place your faith in the Jina,
so that you may uplift yourself from the mire of intoxication and the faults of saṃsāra.
"He who has personally realized the nature of the entire world— come quickly, let us go to the compassionate one!
Then, this thought occurred to Māra, the Evil One, whose mind was utterly wicked:

"What if I were now to recall such a forceful surge of Māra’s power and domain that these five hundred attendants would perceive themselves as bound by fivefold fetters right here and turn back, unable to go further?
Yet Māra was not able to bind them."
How could that be? For those five hundred female attendants were sustained by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
Then those five hundred female attendants departed from the presence of Māra, the Evil One.
Thereupon, Māra, the Evil One, became even more enraged,
and this thought occurred to him:

What if I were now once again to recall such a forceful onset of Māra’s power and domain, so that all this would be enveloped by masses of space-like conflict, great black clouds, and great black winds, such that those very female attendants, bewildered in every direction and intermediate direction, would no longer see the ascetic Gautama?
"May they come to my abode once again!
Even so, by the power of the Buddha’s empowerment, he was unable to produce even a slight breeze—such that it could not shake even the tip of a hair, let alone anything more substantial.

Then Māra the Evil One, becoming even more intensely afflicted with malice, distressed, dejected, and full of regret, weeping aloud and crying out to his sons, hosts, and retinue, [shook] the entire abode of Māra.
He filled [the air] with this sound:
"Come, dear sons, members of the assembly of the Gaṇas!
We have fallen from our own domain and from our own power and miraculous success."
"Born here is this inner self of the son of the Śākyas, like a poison tree; deceitful in his illusory nature, yet sweet of speech.
Then, by that sound, all those daughters of Māra, the daughters of Māra, and all the sons of Māra—(Kurumiya 15)
The hosts of his retinue, assuming hurried and respectful forms, quickly approached and stood before Māra, the Evil One.
In that assembly was a son of Māra named Jayamati;
with palms joined in reverence, he spoke as follows:

Why are you dejected, your mind corrupted by supreme anger? Is there no dissolution of the world here today, nor your own passing from this state? Nor is there any enemy of yours here who has grown powerful.
"You have fallen into delusion; why is your mind so different from others?
Māra replied:
"Do you not see the son of the Śākyas, like a venomous snake, sitting in the shade beneath the tree?"
Regarding the statement you make here in our presence— that there is no powerful enemy for you—
all of us have been repeatedly bewildered by that single, deceitful, and powerful one; we,
along with our sons and the Camaras, are being scorched as if by glowing coals.

Today, all those learned men, who were entirely preoccupied with composing many treatises and poems, have swiftly gone to this son of the Śākyas, drawn forth by the goad of the Dharma. Therefore, this enemy of mine— deceitful-minded, exceedingly arrogant, and fond of conflict— is now subdued.
"O, these most beloved attendants, having abandoned me pitilessly,
have gone today for refuge to that ascetic, even though they made me their witness!"
"Therefore, let this entire triple world be rendered empty by the deceitful one through his magic;
let us today, with great effort, reduce him to ashes here if he is indeed exceedingly powerful.
Then all those sons of Māra, together with their hosts and retinues, joined their palms in reverence and spoke thus:
"So be it! We shall display all the manifestations of our supernatural power, strength, domain, majesty, and miraculous transformations.
If we are able to reduce this son of the Śākyas to ashes, that would be well;
but if we are not able to do so, we shall go to him for refuge."

"Father, you yourself have witnessed firsthand how we, though surrounded by a great army, were previously defeated by this son of the Śākyas alone and without a second companion through the power of his supernatural might; how much more so now that he is surrounded by a vast retinue!
Thus spoke Māra, the Evil One.
"Go now, gentle sirs;
if you are able to kill this ascetic Gautama, then return."
Even if you are not capable, nevertheless come;
we shall protect our own abode once again.

Then, having passed beyond the twelve *biṃbara* assemblies of Māra’s retinue and extending upward for eighty-four thousand *yojanas*, they displayed such a force of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-vega*) belonging to Māra’s army.
They filled the sky throughout all the four continents with great black clouds.
With winds of great duration and the falling of meteors, they struck Sumeru, the king of mountains, with their hands;
they caused the entire system of four continents to tremble and uttered sounds of supreme terror.

Then the *nāgas* and great *nāgas*, the *yakṣas* and great *yakṣas*, having perceived the trembling of the entire great earth with its hills, rocks, and mountains, and of Sumeru, the king of mountains, and having recognized the agitation of the lakes, great lakes, rivers, streams, great rivers, and the great oceans, stood in the expanse of the sky.
And that host of Māra, standing upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, conjured up a rain measuring one *yojana* in depth and released it over Aṅga and Magadha;

and having fashioned a great rain of swords, clubs, stones, spears, javelins, iron arrows, crescent-headed shafts, razor-faced bolts, razor-edged axes, razor-blade wheels, hand-held discs, and revolving discs— all firm, harsh, rough, and coarse— they released it.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One entered the samādhi called "The Destruction of Māra’s Realm. By means of this,
he transformed the entire rain of stone weapons into a rain of divine flowers— blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, *māndārava*, and *mahāmāndārava* flowers—
and he likewise transformed those various sounds of musical instruments.

That is to say, he empowered the sound of "Buddha," the sound of "Dharma," the sound of "Saṅgha," the sound of the "perfections," the sound of the "superknowledges," the sound of the "irreversible," the sound of the "consecration," the sound of the "defeat of the four Māras," the sound of the "approach to the seat of awakening," and so on, up to the sounds of "with grasping" and "without grasping."
All winds carrying dust and darkness were stilled;
whatever grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, trees, earth, stones, and mountains existed here in this world of four continents, he transformed them all into being composed of the seven precious gems.
The Blessed One exercised mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world from his invisible crown;
and from each individual mark of the Blessed One such radiance issued forth, by which radiance the great trichiliocosm was filled with a sublime light.
And all those in this great trichiliocosm—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, humans, and non-humans—[were illuminated].
Whether they were denizens of hell, animals, or inhabitants of the world of Yama, they all beheld the Blessed One.
Many hundreds of thousands of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans, stationed in the sky, scattered flowers, circumambulated him to the right, praised him, and paid homage.
Furthermore, many hundreds of thousands of millions of beings from the realms of hell, animals, and the world of Yama regained their mindfulness.
Recalling the roots of merit planted in the past and having paid homage, saying "Namo Buddhāya," they passed away from those states of woe and were reborn among the gods.

Then, having seen such a miracle performed by the Blessed One, the twenty-two hundred thousand sons of Māra from the army of Māra, together with their hosts and retinues, conceived an exceeding faith in the presence of the Blessed One and approached where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, together with those five hundred daughters of Māra, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed him with these verses:
O you of pure form, O most beautiful one, ocean of wisdom, equal to the golden Mount Meru!
You shine forth, pervading the world with your glory; we go for refuge to you alone, our Lord.
To those who have lost their way and whose eyes are closed, you act as a torch, like the sun to the world.
O sole kinsman of all living beings who are unconquered, we go for refuge to you, the caravan leader.
O one whose treasury of perfected wisdom is well-accumulated, whose mind is liberated from the nature of space and so forth,
whose intention is compassion, and whose speech is affectionate and pleasing— we go for refuge to Sarvārthasiddha.
You are the liberator from the wilderness of saṃsāra, the one who demonstrates cause and effect through their complete assembly;
you dwell in loving-kindness, know the supreme method, and dwell in compassion—we go to you for refuge. (Kurumiya 20) RKP_1.37

In this existence, which resembles an illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water, we take refuge in you, the Lord of the World and King of Physicians, who destroys the sickness of ignorance through non-attachment to sense objects and their bases. You have become a bridge across the midst of the four floods, delivering others by means of the seven riches and the noble conduct.

O friend of the world, who reveals the true path, we worship you here, endowed with compassion. O Hero, Lord, accept our forgiveness for the offense we committed against you, the one of supreme intelligence, when we were corrupted; for you are the sole kinsman and the foremost being in the world.
Having indeed cast off the faction of Māra, we generate the supreme mind of awakening;
we invite all sentient beings, saying, "May we attain the most excellent awakening. (RKP 1.41)
Show us your noble conduct so that we may practice the perfections (*pāramitā*).
By being endowed with how many qualities, free from any falsehood, do they attain awakening?
When we cast flowers before you, let them become parasols in all directions.
"May they remain upon the heads of the best of bipeds in fields that are sources of happiness in all seasons.
Then indeed, all those sons of Māra and daughters of Māra, together with their hosts and retinues, scattered loose flowers over the Blessed One.

And by the supernatural power of the Blessed One, those loose flowers were transformed into many thousands of millions of billions of flower-parasols, more numerous than the sands of the river Gaṅgā, which remained suspended in the air.
Those flower-parasols remained in the sky above the crowns of the heads of all the Buddhas dwelling and maintaining their lives throughout the ten directions.
And those daughters of Māra, together with their hosts and retinues, saw them in all the countless Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions. (Kurumiya 22)

Above, in the sky, at the level of the crowns of the heads of the immeasurable Buddhas, Blessed Ones— who were staying, maintaining themselves, teaching the Dharma, surrounded by assemblies, speaking, blazing, and shining as they sat— those flower-parasols remained suspended. And those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were of identical color, identical marks, identical form, and identical appearance.
They beheld only the diversity of the lion-thrones of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; the diversity of their assemblies; and the diversity of the arrays of qualities of their Buddha-fields.
They also heard the full range of the vocal utterances of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

And that assembly of Māra, having seen such a miraculous display through the power of the Blessed One, was filled with supreme joy and serene faith; they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him.
Then indeed, those sons of Māra, together with their hosts and retinues, having turned back ten billion [beings], reported this news in detail to the evil Māra in his own abode, saying:
"We were not able to destroy even a single pore of that Gautama Śrāvaṇa."
Furthermore, twenty thousand others went to him for refuge and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Then indeed, Māra the Evil One, becoming even more fierce, distressed, dejected, and full of regret, spoke thus:
"Fortune has departed from me and will not return until the destruction of this son of the Śākyas is accomplished.
We have remained silent, our minds intent on no other thought; how indeed shall we [deal with] the son of the Śākyas?"
"But today we shall have him killed. Then Māra the Evil One, dejected, sat down in the chamber of sorrow.
The first chapter of the Mahāyāna Sūtra, titled "The Subduing of Māra by Ratnaketu."
(Kurumiya 24) II.
Then those daughters of Māra and the sons of Māra, together with their hosts and retinues, spoke thus to the Blessed One:

"O Blessed One, we desire such a vehicle as this, and such knowledge, supernatural power, compassion, skillful means, and eloquence. It is marvelous, O Blessed One, how you are endowed with such knowledge of skillful means."
“O Tathāgata,
endowed with what qualities, O Blessed One, does a person not fall into the hands of evil friends and swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Blessed One said: "Sons of good family, endowed with four qualities, a certain person here does not fall into the hands of evil friends and quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
By which four?
Here, noble sirs, a son of good family does not grasp at any phenomena;
nor does he apprehend any phenomenon anywhere, nor take it up, nor dwell upon it, nor conceptualize it, nor discriminate it.

That is to say, while practicing the perfection of generosity, he does not neglect the fruit of generosity; he does not grasp it, does not take it up, does not dwell upon it, and does not conceptualize or discriminate it; and so on, up to when he practices the perfection of wisdom, he likewise does not conceptualize or discriminate.

Furthermore, noble sirs, that son of good family does not advocate for a sentient being (*sattva*), nor for a living soul (*jīva*), nor for a nourisher (*poṣa*), nor for a person (*pudgala*); he does not mentally grasp at the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), nor does he conceptualize it or discriminate it.
Furthermore, noble sirs, that son of good family does not grasp at forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, nor does he conceptualize them or discriminate them.

Furthermore, noble sirs, that son of good family does not grasp at, nor even conceptualize or discriminate, the causes, conditions, objects, fruits, ripenings, arisings, supports, and productions of all the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the three times and the triple world.

Why is that? Because the wisdom of the omniscient one must be practiced through the yoga of non-apprehension, being free from conceptualization and discursive thought regarding the domain of all conduct and its bases.
O noble ones, all phenomena and even omniscience are non-existent; they are soundless, signless, letterless, wishless, unarisen, unceasing, characterless, unattached,

unapprehendable, invisible, secluded, selfless, markless, free from marks, quiescent, without darkness, without light, without location, beyond the sphere of sense-objects, without a lord, without partiality or opposition, inconceivable, without sustenance, without envy, without conceptual proliferation, stainless, free from stain, partless, nothingness, without an agent, without an experiencer, without support, ungraspable, non-cognitive, non-manifesting, and momentary.

"O noble-faced ones, omniscience— which is equal to space— should be practiced through the yoga of emptiness and non-apprehension, the yoga of non-abiding, the yoga of non-clinging, and the yoga of non-conceptualization and non-discrimination."
O friends, a person endowed with these four qualities does not fall into the hands of evil companions and swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"O noble ones, whoever seeks the knowledge of the Omniscient One by means of investigating the basis characterized by the elevation of attachment to all sense objects becomes attached to duality.
A mental intention attached to duality deceives omniscience.
In that regard, what is duality?"
To dwell upon and grasp the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields through the investigation of their characteristics—this is duality; it deceives all-knowledge.
The conceptualization of the practice, its basis, and its fruit—this is duality.
The conceptualization of birth, existence, grasping, and sentient beings as bases—this is duality.
The conceptualization of the basis of speech, sounds, and utterances—consisting of teaching, revealing, and establishing—is duality.
The conceptualization of the basis of knowledge and the knowable—consisting of the contemplation of annihilation and permanence—is duality.
The conceptualization of the basis of notions—consisting of sentient being, life-force, nourisher, person, individual, agent, and instigator—is duality.
"O friends, whoever presides over or conceptualizes the taking up and the discarding of the far and the near—this is duality.

Any person who seeks the knowledge of an omniscient one, O friends, presides over, conceptualizes, discriminates, and grasps the arising and cessation of the notions of 'I' and 'mine' regarding the three times; for him, this is duality with respect to the knowledge of an omniscient one."

It is, for example, as if some man seeking fire were to grasp at the ground; one seeking drink were to grasp at fire; one seeking food were to grasp at a stone; one seeking flowers were to grasp at a robe; one seeking fragrance were to grasp at a human corpse; one seeking clothing were to grasp at a rock;
and one seeking ointment were to grasp at space.
In the same way, noble sirs, whoever seeks the knowledge of omniscience by means of the dual basis—the attachment to and investigation of the foundation of conduct—his exertion is fruitless.
Then, indeed, in that very assembly, a bodhisattva named Dhāraṇamati was present and seated. Bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he spoke thus:
"That which is ineffable—can it be fully awakened to?"
The Blessed One said: "This very thing is perfect awakening: that one knows what is inexpressible.
Therefore, noble son, I shall explain it to you."
"Answer as you see fit:
Is there a substantial entity that receives the name 'omniscience'?
He replied, "If I say that it exists, it will become eternal."
If, on the other hand, I were to say that it does not exist, there would be nihilism;
furthermore, the Middle Way would not be found.
"It neither exists nor does it not exist":
that knowledge regarding these [dharmas]—which are unattached, unarisen, undecaying, immeasurable, incalculable, and the light of wisdom—is itself perfect awakening.
The bodhisattva Vidyunmati said:
"Blessed One, that skill in entering into knowledge such that there is neither coming nor going—this itself is perfect awakening."

The Bodhisattva Vairocana said: "O Blessed One, where there is neither the characteristic of attainment nor the characteristic of non-attainment, neither realization nor direct realization, neither tranquility nor complete pacification, neither the three times nor the three vehicles, and neither the conceit of aspiration nor of propriety— this indeed is perfect awakening."
The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇamati said:

"O Blessed One, he who does not conceptualize or discriminate the triple world, nor the three fetters, nor the state of the three knowledges, nor the three vehicles, nor the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; who perceives neither decrease nor increase, and does not perform acts of formal compliance."
This indeed is perfect awakening.

The bodhisattva Vajramati said: "He who does not conceptualize, does not discriminate, and does not treat as real the dharmas of ordinary beings, the dharmas of the noble ones, the dharmas of those in training, the dharmas of those beyond training, the dharmas of śrāvakas, and the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas—
this indeed is perfect awakening."
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati said:
"For one who investigates suchness by means of the method of seclusion, this itself is perfect awakening."
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said:
"He who does not conceptualize the non-arising characteristic of all dharmas, nor [strives] for their attainment or realization—this alone is perfect awakening."
The Bodhisattva Acintyamati said:

"That which is the investigation of the three realms—when one causes the mind itself to enter into the mind, and having investigated both minds with the mind, does not perceive them—this indeed is perfect awakening."
The Bodhisattva Arivijaya said:

"That which does not cling to any phenomena, is not led by them, does not neglect them, is not repelled by them, does not crave them, is not deluded by them, does not grasp them, and is not released from them— this alone is perfect awakening."
The Bodhisattva Padmagarbha said:
"He who does not cling to merit or demerit, and by entering into the method of profound patience does not conceptualize 'I' and 'mine'—this indeed is perfect awakening."
The youth Candraprabha said:

"He who does not perceive all phenomena as being like the moon reflected in water, and who does not see the intrinsic nature of phenomena, nor their accumulation or diminution—this indeed is perfect awakening."
The youth Khagamati said:
"That in which the arising and passing away, the increase and decrease of all darkness and light do not occur within the mind and mental factors—this alone is perfect awakening."
The Bodhisattva Maitreya said:
"This very thing is perfect awakening."
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said:
"He who practices the perfections through the purity of the three spheres, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension, neither becomes attached nor becomes detached—this indeed is perfect awakening."
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said:
“Blessed One, he who is neither attached to nor detached from all phenomena understands the profound principle of the Dharma.
And that which he understands, he neither accumulates nor discards, neither draws in nor draws out, and he does not effect the increase of any phenomenon whatsoever.”

Whether it be accumulation or diminution, knowledge or liberation, arising or passing away, loss or increase regarding phenomena, one does not become afflicted because of non-conceptualization; this indeed is perfect awakening.
By this manifold method, there is the perfect awakening to the wisdom of omniscience.
Then the Bodhisattva Kautūhalika said:

"Mañjuśrī, what is the purpose of application and practice, since through this very entry into the single principle of suchness and by means of this method of cultivating profound emptiness, there is the full comprehension of the knowledge of the omniscient one?"
Mañjuśrī said: "It is being free from uneven views, the non-superimposition of right view, and the non-superimposition of guilelessness and rectitude."
Freedom from evil; the non-attribution of undue weight to the teacher; the non-attribution of [excessive] compliance to pleasant speech; and the non-attribution of [faults to] right livelihood.
It is the non-superimposition of being free from all fetters;
it is the superimposition of compassion for all beings toward those who revile one;
it is the non-superimposition of the three vows.
Non-deception, the non-superimposition of unwholesome dharmas,
the non-superimposition of non-quiescence,
and the superimposition of the protection of the true Dharma.
The non-superimposition of not abandoning any sentient being; the non-superimposition of relinquishing all things;
the non-superimposition of establishing strength in weak sentient beings.
The supererogatory application of granting fearlessness as a refuge to those who are afraid; the supererogatory application of enjoining those set out on wrong paths to the correct practice;
and the supererogatory application of patience and gentleness.
It is the non-superimposition of the characteristics of all grasping and attachment; it is the non-superimposition of the avoidance of all masses of passion and ignorance;
it is the non-superimposition of the avoidance of the ripening of the fruits of all dedications.
Noble son, these twenty applications are for the sake of the knowledge of omniscience.
Through the entry into the knowledge of suchness regarding the distinctions of all syllables, sounds, voices, speech, and phrases, they are the applications for the knowledge of omniscience;
through the entry into the suchness of the words of all Tathāgatas and the words of non-Buddhist teachers, and through the entry into the suchness of all conduct.

By entering into the suchness of the application of all perfections of merit and wisdom, by entering into the suchness of the arising and passing away of all appropriation, and by entering into the suchness of the dharmas of cause, karma, and basis of all three liberations, one comes to realize the application of the knowledge of the omniscient one.

The Bodhisattva Kautūhalika said: "It is so, Mañjuśrī. When one realizes this profound method of the Dharma, then one does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever—that phenomenon which might be taught, for whom it might be taught, or by means of which meanings, phrases, and syllables it might be taught or revealed."
Furthermore, whatever one may abandon, whatever one may cultivate, or whatever one may fully comprehend—
by means of the yoga of the ineffability of all phenomena— one enters into suchness, which is the realization of the knowledge of the omniscient one.
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, noble son! This attainment of the knowledge of the omniscient one by means of the single principle has been well-spoken by you.
Why is that? Because all phenomena are indeed without superimposition, having the limit of non-arising and non-destruction."

All phenomena have the limit of non-ignorance, the limit of nirvāṇa, the limit of non-arising, the limit of the reality-limit, and the limit of space-like nirvāṇa; they have the limit of the ineffable. So too do all sentient beings.

(Kurumiya 32) All phenomena are proclaimed to be the limit of substancelessness, because they are devoid of all objects of attachment; they are the limit of the lack of anything substantial within the aggregates of the three times and the three realms;
they are the limit of the emptiness of the three types of conditioned formations.
Endowed with the aggregates of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*), the aggregates of maturation (*vipākaskandha*), the aggregates of decrease and increase (*apacayopacayaskandha*),

the limit of non-substantiality (*adravyakoṭi*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the ineffable meaning of all phenomena (*anabhilāpyārtha*), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters into the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Furthermore, while this prophecy regarding the attainment of the knowledge of the omniscient one was being spoken, twenty thousand members of the retinue consisting of hosts of Māra’s daughters and Māra’s sons attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Abandoning their coarse bodies, they obtained mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
Twenty-eight others also attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
and ninety-two billion beings among gods and humans attained various and manifold bodhisattva patiences, samādhis, and dhāraṇīs.
Then those twenty thousand bodhisattva mahāsattvas who had attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena scattered and strewed divine flowers over the Blessed One;
and having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they spoke as follows:
"Behold, Blessed One, how by the power of association with unwholesome friends, the roots of merit consisting of the accumulation of all virtues become objects of non-attention for sentient beings.
The Blessed One said:
This should be understood as having karma as its condition;
and for the sake of cutting through the doubts of those beings who had come out of curiosity, the Blessed One recounted this former account.
Long ago, son of good family, in the past, after immeasurable great eons had passed, in this very world-system of four continents, at that time and at that moment,
while the great eon called Dyutindhara was occurring and when the lifespan of beings was sixty-eight thousand years—
at that time and at that moment— there appeared a Tathāgata named Jyotiḥsomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī.
There appeared one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
While the world was abiding in the afflicted age of five corruptions, he taught the Dharma connected with the three vehicles to the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, at that time there was a king named Utpalavaktra, a universal monarch (cakravartin) who ruled over the four continents.
Then, on another occasion, King Utpalavaktra, together with his retinue of queens and his army, went toward Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī.
He approached the Tathāgata; having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of that Blessed One and scattered various flowers over the Blessed One.

Having performed worship with various musical instruments, various perfumes, and various incenses, and having circumambulated him three times, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and the community of monks, and praised him with these two verses:
Extolled exceedingly by the nāgas, gods, and others for his supreme qualities, the remover of manifold faults,
and the benefactor of the world through the seven riches— tell me, by what means does one become possessed of subtle intelligence?
O destroyer of the world’s darkness, maker of the lamp of tranquility, tamer of the grief of birth, death, and disease for the world—
since you are the one who blocks the path to the lower realms for the world, tell me: by what means here is one liberated from the path of Māra?
Then, noble son, that Tathāgata Jyotiḥsomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī spoke thus to King Utpalavaktra:
Bodhisattva endowed with three qualities of a true person becomes one of subtle intelligence.
Which three? He feels compassion for all sentient beings with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*).
He exerts himself like a mother for the sake of pacifying the suffering of all sentient beings;
he thoroughly examines all phenomena as being without a life-principle, without a nourisher, without a person, and as equal in their lack of differentiation.
Endowed with these three qualities, the true person, the bodhisattva, becomes one of subtle intelligence.
Furthermore, Great King, a virtuous person endowed with three other qualities becomes ensnared in the snares of Māra.
What are these three? Namely, he is free from anger toward all sentient beings.
He does not look for an opportunity to enter [into faults];
he regards all sentient beings as equal objects of veneration;
and he examines all phenomena through a single principle.
That is to say, he contemplates all phenomena as equal to space—requiring no recompense, without differentiation, unborn, unarisen, and unceasing;
he observes them all, like space, as devoid of substantial characteristics by means of non-apprehension.
Great King, a true person endowed with these three qualities is not ensnared by the snares of Māra and is liberated from the path of Māra.
Then the chief queen of King Utpalavaktra, named Surasundarī, surrounded and escorted by eighty-four thousand women,
approached the Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī. Having arrived,
she scattered various flowers over that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī, and paid him homage.
He addressed him with verses.
O bearer of incomparable qualities, O dispeller of darkness, O remover of rebirth, tell me how one may become a man here;
O Blessed One, how can a man here abandon that young woman?
Speak quickly, O you who are well-disciplined and devoted to the welfare of others.
Quell the darkness of my ignorance from the sky!
O Śramaṇa, peerless in this world, supreme one who possesses a multitude of renowned virtues and maintains mindfulness and discipline— if, moreover, for me...
"In this world, human existence is indeed fleeting; speak quickly the nectar of the path to the stainless, happy realms.
When this was said, O son of good family, that Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī spoke thus to his chief queen, Surasundarī.

"Sister, there is a method by which a woman quickly transforms her female state; her previously projected female state is swiftly and completely exhausted, and she no longer takes rebirth among women until her unsurpassed final nirvana,
except by her own vow."
In this regard, sister, what is the method by which a woman quickly becomes a man and swiftly exhausts, without remainder, the female state previously projected?

Here, sister, is this dhāraṇī called Ratnaketu, which is of great purpose, great benefit, and great power; it brings about the end of all female states and exhausts, without remainder, the corruption consisting of the ripening of suffering in body, speech, and mind.
And upon merely hearing this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, the female state of a woman passes away without remainder;
the female faculty disappears and the male faculty appears.
Furthermore, that man becomes handsome, with all his limbs fully perfected.
He becomes upright and skilled in subtle knowledge;
with his bodily, vocal, and mental actions well-performed, he practices right conduct and becomes a conqueror of all enemies.
And as for whatever [result] of his evil deeds is to be experienced as suffering of body, speech, and mind, pertaining both to the present life and to future lives—

That ripening of the fruit comes to an end, with the exception of those who have committed the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), those who reject the true Dharma, and those who slander the Noble Ones;
for them, however, it comes to an end within that very same lifetime.

The remainder consists of the female state, which is the result of the maturation of the corruption of body, speech, and mind, as vast as Mount Sumeru, pertaining to future lives, and productive of the seed of the female state.
The outflow of the seeds of karmic obstructions that result in the experience of painful retribution goes to complete exhaustion without remainder.
Why is that?
Because this *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī* has been [proclaimed] by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past.

It has been spoken, empowered, mutually rejoiced in, praised, extolled, described, and lauded for the sake of exhausting the karma that ripens as suffering for sentient beings and for the increase of their roots of merit.
Furthermore, whatever Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas there may be at present in the ten directions—

All those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who currently abide and maintain themselves in their respective Buddha-fields, are reciting this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī and even praising it for the sake of exhausting the karma of sentient beings and for the increase of their roots of virtue.
Furthermore, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future in various directions throughout the ten quarters— [they too shall do so].

They too shall speak this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, even up to praising it, for the sake of exhausting the karma that results in the suffering of sentient beings and for the increase of their roots of merit;
I, too, shall now speak the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī.
And having rejoiced, I shall praise and extol this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī for the Tathāgatas currently residing and teaching in the ten directions.

Sister, if any consecrated Kṣatriya king who has attained power over his realm should write down this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī in a book and preserve it, that Kṣatriya king’s noble fame, renown, and verses of praise will spread throughout the ten directions.
He shall rise up and fill the entire realm of form with his magnificent renown and fame;
and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas shall follow behind that kṣatriya king, remaining there for his protection and guardianship.
And in his domain, all the defects of strife, quarrels, famine, disease, foreign armies, wind, rain, cold, and heat shall cease.
They shall all become pacified;
and all wicked yakṣas, rākṣasas, lions, buffaloes, elephants, and wolves shall cease to cause harm.
All defects that are to be experienced as painful sensations—characterized by poison, bitterness, pungency, coarseness, lack of flavor, harshness, and suffering—shall come to rest.
Furthermore, all his wealth, grain, medicinal herbs, trees, fruits, and flowers will sprout, flourish, and become succulent and delicious.
If a consecrated Kṣatriya king, when a battle has arisen, should place this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī book upon the tip of a banner, that consecrated Kṣatriya king will defeat the enemy army.
If this manuscript of the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī is hoisted upon the top of the banner of two consecrated Kṣatriya kings who have entered into battle, they will establish mutual affection and harmony.
Thus, this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī possesses many such qualities and benefits.

In whatever village, city, or market town there may be, where humans, non-humans, or four-footed creatures suffer from disease, untimely death, or affliction, this manuscript of the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī should be brought therein with great offerings and requisites.
Having brought it in, by one who is well-bathed, whose limbs are well-anointed, who is clad in new robes, who observes celibacy, and who is fanned with various flowers—
Having ascended a lion throne perfumed with various incenses and surrounded by various delicacies, this manuscript of the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī should be recited there;
all diseases and untimely deaths therein will be pacified. All [these]... (Kurumiya 41)
And therein, all fears, horripilation, and ill omens shall disappear.

Whatever woman may desire a son, she should bathe, don new robes, and, observing celibacy, honor this book with flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ointments; she herself [should sit] amidst various flowers being scattered and various perfumes being burned as incense.
Having ascended a seat adorned with various flavors, this *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī* should be recited;
one will obtain a son.
This shall be her final existence as a woman, until her unsurpassed parinirvāṇa, except for the sake of ripening sentient beings through her own vow.

having ascended the marks of a superior person:
amame vamame vamame.

Jalamekha / Parakha / Alajahili.
O people, weigh! O people, eat! Eat, eat!
In the Siṃha-vrata: nine sesame seeds, nine grains of rice, and nine pulses.
O bird of the sun!
O bird of the moon!

Vahama / Amrikha / Amrikha.

in each and every [instance],
the interruption is produced by knowledge.

and toward [it].
And [he spoke] regarding non-delusion and right vision;
he preached the turning of the wheel.
Equal to space / O bird of the light of the stars / Depart, depart, O light!
Niṣkabhirasa, bhirasa, bhiraja.
Matikrama / Bhivakriva / Mahākriva.

Through self-restraint, generosity, and meditation, do not touch upon [worldly things];
O you who possess the marks of a fruit and earrings, turn back from the state of womanhood! Through the exhaustion of karma, let manhood manifest.
O Peerless One, Knower of the Time, Tathāgata, svāhā!
As soon as this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī was spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the great earth shook once again.
Upon hearing this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, the female characteristics of those five hundred daughters of Māra vanished and male characteristics appeared.
This also occurred for immeasurable and incalculable daughters of the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, and kumbhāṇḍas.
Upon hearing this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, the female characteristics of those women vanished and male characteristics appeared;
they all became irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
and the karmic obstructions of all of them that would have led to the acquisition of a female state in the future were extinguished without remainder.
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence to that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, those women spoke thus with resonant voices:
Homage, homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, the performer of wonders!
"Speak in detail, O Great Compassionate One, of this former life: how was our female state made to disappear and how did we attain a male state complete in all its aspects?
Through the inspiration of that wondrous miracle, may we generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Speak, Blessed One, of this former life."
He will be the witness for that immeasurable one, who is both god and human.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, taught this former account: "O noble ones,
in the presence of the Tathāgata Jyotiḥsomagandhāvabhāsaśrī, King Utpalavaktra’s chief queen, the goddess Surasundarī,
together with eighty-four thousand women, heard this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī."
Upon hearing the name of that chief queen, Surasundarī,
the female characteristics of those eighty-four thousand women vanished and male characteristics appeared.

Likewise, at the very moment of hearing this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī, the female organs of immeasurable and incalculable numbers of celestial maidens, up to and including human and non-human maidens, disappeared and male organs appeared.
When it had appeared,
the karmic obstructions of all those women that would have led to the acquisition of female existence in the future were completely and utterly extinguished.

And when the chief queen of King Utpalavaktra, Surasundarī, together with her retinue of women, was transformed into a man, then King Utpalavaktra, the universal monarch (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents, consecrated his eldest son with the royal inauguration and,
together with his nine hundred and ninety-nine sons and the great man Surasundara, [departed] along with eighty-four...
Surasundara, together with thousands of great men and another ninety-two thousand living beings, having gone forth,
shaved off his hair and beard in the presence of that Tathāgata Jyotiḥsomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī, donned saffron robes, and out of perfect faith went forth from the home to the homeless life.
Having gone forth, he became devoted to recitation and dedicated to appropriate mental attention.
Then, this thought occurred to many millions of living beings there:
"Why has the universal monarch gone forth into the religious life?
They said this to one another:

"This Tathāgata is engaged in the works of Māra; he is deceitful and a magician who teaches this Dharma associated with the works of Māra. To some he causes the female characteristics to disappear, and to others the male characteristics."
For some he causes the hair and beard to be shaved;
to some he gives red robes, and to others white ones;
for some he teaches the Dharma for the sake of rebirth as a god.
He teaches the Dharma for some to be reborn as humans, for others to be reborn in the animal realm, and for others to be reborn in the state of non-retrogression;

yet he is devoted to the paths of Māra’s deeds and possesses the illusion of assuming a female form. This Śravaṇa, who shines with the splendor of light, moon, and fragrance, is a deceiver appearing in the guise of a śramaṇa.
Let us therefore depart from here.
Nor do we perceive the grasping of his form or signs,
nor do we hear any speech from him.
Then, right there, a soldier named Kumārabhṛta spoke thus:
"By this wretched śramaṇa Koṇḍaka, all those who were my wives, women of the harem, and daughters— " (Kurumiya 46)
Having removed the female characteristics, male organs were manifested;
having shaved the heads of all of them, red garments were bestowed upon them,
while I alone was released, afflicted with grief.

"All of us together shall enter that rugged and vast mountain wilderness where we shall not even hear the sound of the voice of this deceptive ascetic, this crow-like ascetic ensnared by the noose of Māra, let alone see him.
All of them, being thus delighted, spoke as follows.
"So be it."

Then the soldier Kumārabhṛta, together with those many tens of millions of beings who were seized by doubt, departed from there and went to the borderlands; in the rugged mountain thickets, he lived the life of a wandering ascetic in the guise of a ṛṣi,
and he taught the Dharma to those very beings in this way:
"There is no liberation from saṃsāra; there is no ripening of the fruit of well-done or ill-done deeds.

Today a śramaṇa has arisen who is a proponent of annihilationism, intent on the works of Māra, and a deceiver. Those who approach him for a vision, those who pay him homage, and those who listen to his Dharma become distracted in mind."
He shaves their heads,
drives them out of their homes,
and gives them red garments.
He practices the conduct of the charnel ground;
he establishes himself in the practice of begging for alms;
he makes himself a consumer of a single meal per day.

He makes those who possess uneven views and minds, who are constantly agitated, who delight in dwelling in seclusion, and who have entered their retreats— those devoid of sensual pleasure, dancing, singing, perfumes, garlands, ointments, ornaments, finery, sexual intercourse, and the drinking of wine and liquor— to be speakers of little speech.
In such a form, he has appeared as one wearing the garb of a śramaṇa, a proponent of annihilationism, intent on the path of Māra, and an enemy to sentient beings.

"I have observed the deeds of this śramaṇa Gautama, the likes of which have never been seen or heard before," [he thought], and by him many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of living beings were made to adopt such an evil view.

Then, at another time, the great ascetic Utpalavaktra heard that in a certain mountain thicket some people had themselves set out upon a wrong path and were leading others astray, causing them to adopt this same perilous view and spreading disrepute regarding the Three Jewels. Upon hearing this, the thought occurred to him:
"If I were not to liberate these beings from those evil views and establish them in right view, my life as a śramaṇa would be in vain.

And how could I, in a future time when the world has become blind, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? And how shall I be able to liberate beings who have fallen into calamity, bound by the fetters of the snares of the four Māras?"

Then the great śramaṇa Utpalavaktra, possessed of great and firm prowess and full of compassion, beheld the Tathāgata Jyotiḥsomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī; surrounded and honored by hundreds of thousands of many living beings,
he wandered on his tour through various outlying villages, cities, market towns, mountains, rugged terrains, and mountain hamlets, [teaching] to those sentient beings in each of those places.
He taught the Dharma;
having turned those beings away from evil views and established them in right view, he settled them in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Some others he established in the aspiration for the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, some in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, and some in the fruits [of the path].

He caused some to go forth [into homelessness], established some in the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), some in the fast-day observance (*upavāsa*), and some in the taking of the three refuges. [He did likewise] for women. (Kurumiya 48)
He taught this Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī;
having turned them back from their female state, he established them in manhood.
And as for those many millions of living beings who had fallen into doubt in the presence of the Tathāgata, he [established] them all [in certainty].
Then, having turned him away from that evil state of view and having caused him to confess his transgression, he established him in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and having set aside the soldier Kumārabhṛta, he brought him into the presence of that very Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī and ordained him as a monk.
And he made this vow:

"Just as this ascetic Utpalavaktra has led away and dispersed my assembly, so too shall I exercise the office of Māra in that buddha-field when he has set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— starting from the very moment of his conception in the womb."
"Starting from this moment, I shall harass him;

thereafter, I shall strike terror into him and create obstacles at every stage—from his birth, while he is being entertained as a child, while he is engaged in the arts and studies, while he is in the midst of sensual pleasures and the inner apartments, up until he is seated at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa); and once he has attained awakening, I shall bring about the destruction of his teaching."

Then that great śramaṇa Utpalavaktra, having won over the soldier Kumārabhṛta— who was thus resolved upon his vow— through great hardship, exertion, and valor, turned him back from that evil state of view, caused him to confess his transgression, and inspired in him the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then the soldier Kumārabhṛta, his faith having been subdued, made this aspiration:

"When you, O Great Compassionate One, have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then, having attained awakening, may you prophesy my own attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, O gentle sirs, you may perhaps have some doubt or uncertainty that at that time,

on that occasion, the one named Utpalavaktra— who performed manifold kinds of worship and service for that Tathāgata Jyotisomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī together with his retinue, along with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings— was someone else. [He was not.]

Having gone forth together [with him], he renounced the world; and having turned away hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of immeasurable living beings from those evil views, he established them in the three vehicles, set immeasurable beings in the fruits [of the path],
and brought about the attainment of manhood for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of women.
Indeed, you should not view it in this way.
At that time, on that occasion, I was the king, the universal monarch (cakravartin) who ruled over the four continents, named Utpalavaktra.
It was by me that such an office of authority over men was exercised.
Furthermore, O gentle sirs, you might perhaps have some doubt or uncertainty: was she who at that time, on that occasion, was the chief queen named Surasundarī anyone else?
It was indeed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya who, at that time, on that occasion, became a renunciant.

Furthermore, O gentle sirs, you might perhaps have some doubt or uncertainty: was he who at that time, on that occasion, was the soldier named Kumārabhṛta, together with tens of millions of living beings, anyone else? [He was none other than myself.]
Furthermore, you must not view it in this way:
at that time, on that occasion, that wicked Māra was the soldier named Kumārabhṛta.
Because his assembly went forth [into homelessness] under me at that time, he conceived malice toward me and made this vow.
When you have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, then you should grant me the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Sons of good family, it was because you had conceived a lack of faith toward that very Tathāgata Jyotiḥsomyagandhāvabhāsaśrī and had embraced evil views and unrestrained speech that I liberated you from those evil views and caused you to go forth into the religious life.
Prior to that, you have attended upon many thousands of Buddhas;
you have performed worship and service for them,
and having heard the Dharma from them, you have made aspirations and practiced the six perfections.
Because of that karma consisting of misconduct of body, speech, and mind, you previously experienced sufferings in the three lower realms for many eons;
by that very same karmic obstruction, you have now been reborn in the abode of Māra, the Evil One.

Furthermore, while this *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-pūrvayoga* was being spoken by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the female forms of those five hundred daughters of Māra disappeared and they were transformed into male forms; they attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and so did immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of beings, including gods and humans. (Kurumiya 51)
The minds of the assembly were set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and they became irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Likewise, immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings became irreversible in the vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
For immeasurable and incalculable daughters of gods and humans, their female state was eliminated, and they obtained a basis in the male state.
The second chapter, the Chapter on the Previous Deeds, from the Ratnaketuparivarta, is completed.

Now, while this *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī* was being spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, this entire Sahā world-system was suffused with a sublime radiance.

And within this buddha-field, there were a hundred koṭis of four-continent worlds (*cāturdvīpika*), and in those [worlds], a hundred koṭis of Māras who exercise lordship over the realm of desire (*kāmeśvara*) were reigning as Māras.
Through the power of the Buddhas, they became agitated and surveyed this world-system of four continents, wondering, "From where has this radiance arisen?
Surely it is the power of that one called Māra the Evil One who dwells here in this world-system of four continents; he must be stronger than we, more powerful, and possessed of greater majesty."
Then indeed, those Māras, looking about, saw that Māra the Evil One seated in the chamber of grief, extremely dejected in mind.
Then those one hundred million Māras went toward this world-system of four continents, to where the abode of the evil Māra was; having approached, they spoke thus to the evil Māra:
"O Lord of Desire, why is it that this entire world-system has been illuminated, while you have entered your chamber of sorrow and sit there?"
(Kurumiya 53) Then Kāmeśvara Māra announced in detail to those hundreds of millions of Māras:
"O friends, you should know that here has arisen from the Śākya clan a most deceitful and illusory ascetic."
As soon as he was born, this entire Sahā world-system was illuminated, shaken, and stirred.

Whatever beings there were here in this entire world-system— whether Brahma-lords, Indra-lords, Naga-lords, Yaksha-lords, Asura-lords, Mahoraga-lords, Garuda-lords, Kinnara-lords, or even any others, whether human or non-human— they all [were affected].
All those wise ones approached him for the purpose of worship; meanwhile, for six years, he alone and without a second sat down and accomplished the *māyā* characterized by immovability.

And I, desiring to display my own power, having approached with a retinue of an army of thirty-six *koṭis*, surrounded him on all sides, and displayed within a single pore of his skin the entire miraculous power, vigor, and prowess of the forces of Māra.
"Am I even incapable of terrifying or frightening him, let alone shaking him from his seat,
much less causing him any other harm?"— this was his thought when that low-born man displayed such an illusion and caused the earth to tremble.
Because I was defeated along with my army and fell to the surface of the earth like a felled tree,

he remained seated right there and accomplished such a signless illusion (*alakṣaṇā māyā*) that, having mastered the vidyā which overcomes the entire domain of Māra, he rose up from it and revealed it to all sentient beings.

And whatever wise and discerning beings there are here in this world-system of four continents who are thus captivated by that illusion— such that I do not even know their minds, nor their destiny or rebirth among the six realms of existence—
I am unable to terrify or disturb even a single pore of those who have gone for refuge to him, let alone deceive them or cause them to tremble.
Or rather,

this very day my five hundred female attendants and twenty thousand sons, together with their hosts and retinues, have gone for refuge to that low-born ascetic Gautama and are seated before him; therefore, I am no longer able to separate them from him.
"Therefore, may you become powerful, meritorious, wise, sovereign, and well-favored.
We shall deprive that low-born son of the Śākyas of his life;
and we shall utterly destroy all those beings who have gone for refuge to him."
(Kurumiya 55) We shall defeat the dark faction of the ascetics, who are deceitful and fraudulent;

The Evil One said:
"My people have indeed been brought under control, for these people of yours now follow his lead.
Before long he will make our realm empty; where then will our refuge be?"
Then the Māra named Navarajas said this to the Evil Māra:
"When you possessed supreme prosperity, you displayed your own heroism;

Khaḍgasoma Māra said:
"In no way does he possess mental malice, for he is pure in being and without support;
his movement through the realms of the three worlds is liberated, and indeed, he cannot be slain by others."
The Evil One said:
"Those beings here in this realm of desire who are attached to sensual pleasures and are intoxicated by pride and conceit; [they are the ones you seek to save]."
"My servants have always followed me; how could it not be possible for all of them to kill him?
Thus spoke the Māra named Kṣititoya. [The Buddha replied:
"Having fully understood that phenomena are essence-less, like illusions and mirages, he has subdued his thirst."
"Unattached to states of existence and having the nature of space—how could it be possible to cause him any harm?

Thus spoke the Māra named Tṛṣṇājaha.

The Māra named Durdharṣa spoke thus:
"We shall strive to destroy those who are bound by the snares of the three fetters;
but how indeed can he, whose snares of illness and delusion have been abandoned, be brought to destruction?"
The Evil One said:
"O you who have attained power, become my allies this very moment; remain vigilant!
I shall command the waters, the entire earth without exception, and all the directions garlanded with mountains."
From the sky, I shall unleash a fierce rain of clouds and mountains, and a heap of iron filings;
I shall hurl iron arrows, spears, razors, and javelins at his body in order to pulverize it.
By these applications, blazing with destructive force, I shall reduce that Lion of the Śākyas to ashes.
And so on, until ten million Māras had spoken ten million verses.
Then all the Māras spoke with one voice:
"So be it."
"We shall go!
Having donned our armor from our respective abodes, we shall come accompanied by our armies and retinues;
we shall display everything that falls within the scope of our supernatural power and strength."
Then you will see for yourself what kind of heroism that ascetic Gautama will display at that moment.

Thereupon, those tens of millions of Māras went to their own abodes, donned their armor, and each Māra, accompanied by a retinue of thousands of millions, put on various types of mail and was equipped with diverse weapons,
arrayed in various kinds of armor.

meanwhile, all those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, and kumbhāṇḍas within this world-system of four continents who had minds lacking faith toward the Blessed One, whose thoughts were devoid of reverence and attention, and who lacked faith in the Dharma and the Saṃgha— [all these were gathered].
All of them were incited by Māra the Evil One to kill the Blessed One; yet,
though they stood right there clad in various armor and equipped with weapons,
Māra the Evil One went to the side of the Himalayas, where the seer Jyotīrasa dwelt, a devotee of Maheśvara.

Having attained mastery over the eighteen branches of knowledge and the sphere of supernatural powers, he stood before him with a retinue of five hundred and, assuming the form of Maheśvara, spoke thus: "O wise one,

Relying on the superknowledges,

And all those Māra-kumārakas, running along with Śāriputra to the sound of singing, spoke thus:

For the sense-bases are slaughterhouses; I shall bring an end to the sense-bases."

Even so, fifty Māra youths spoke thus with melodic voices:

For these elements are indeed places of slaughter; I shall bring an end to those things made of elements.
Enough indeed with sensations, for I have been deceived by sensations;
sensations are indeed places of slaughter; I shall bring an end to sensations.
Enough indeed with volitions, for we have been deceived by volitions;
for volitions are like slaughterhouses—I shall bring an end to volitions.
Enough indeed with conceptual constructions, for we have been deceived by conceptual constructions.
For these places of slaughter are created by conceptualization; I shall bring an end to those things created by conceptualization.

Those, however, who cultivate the single principle—which is devoid of possessions and free from all signs—[attain the same].

Having analyzed all phenomena here as empty, without an owner, and devoid of an agent,

Then, when Māra saw that all those Māras together with their retinues had gone for refuge to the ascetic Gautama, he became even more agitated, terrified, and bewildered; weeping aloud, he spoke as follows: (Kurumiya 82)
"I have no further companion; my glory is lost today in every respect.
I have fallen from the realm of Māra; therefore, I shall exert my final vigor.
I will cut the lotus from its very root, so that sentient beings may depart for the various directions."
"Because the lotus has been severed, they are bewildered; this must be the final power [of Māra].

Having thought thus, Māra the Evil One descended from the sky like the wind, moved toward where that lotus lay upon the path, and advancing there, he desired to uproot the lotus from its stalk, yet he was not even able to touch it.
He wished to pluck the petals but could not see them;
he even wished to strike the pericarp of the lotus with his hand, yet he could not find it at all.
Just as lightning is seen but not apprehended,
or just as a shadow is seen but not apprehended,
even so that lotus is seen but not apprehended.
And when Māra the Evil One saw that lotus, he could neither grasp it nor touch it.
Then, wishing again to let out a loud, most terrifying cry in order to terrify the entire assembly, even then he was unable to do so.
Furthermore, with great force and speed, he wished to strike the great earth with both hands and shake it, yet he was unable to touch it or grasp it at all.
It was just as if someone wished to grasp at space but could not find it;
in the same way, Māra the Evil One saw the earth, yet he neither touched it nor found it. This thought occurred to him:
"Suppose now that I were to strike these assembled beings or cause them mental distraction," he thought; however, he looked at those beings and did not perceive even a single being.
